lines.text: America's a net oil seller. So why did gas hit $4.47?
lines.say: America's a net oil seller. So why did gas hit four forty-seven?

lines.text: The answer is one global price, and it ripples into your flights, your packages, and your groceries.
lines.say: The answer is one global price, and it ripples into your flights, your packages, and eventually your groceries.

lines.text: Since 2020, the US has exported more petroleum than it imports. In 2025, about 2.8 million barrels a day more.
lines.say: Since twenty twenty, the US has exported more petroleum than it imports. In twenty twenty-five, it was about two point eight million barrels a day more.

lines.text: And still, on September 28, 2026, regular gas averaged about $4.47 a gallon, $1.35 more than a year earlier.
lines.say: And still, on September twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six, regular gas averaged about four forty-seven a gallon. That's a dollar thirty-five more than a year earlier.

lines.text: That's not a mistake. Oil trades on one world market, and every country pays roughly the same price for it.
lines.say: That's not a mistake. Oil trades on one world market, and every country pays roughly the same price for it.

lines.text: So let's follow a barrel from a tanker to your checkout line, with real numbers at every step.
lines.say: So let's follow one barrel, from a tanker all the way to your checkout line, with real numbers at every step.

lines.text: Chapter one. One world price.
lines.say: Chapter one. One world price.

lines.text: A barrel is 42 gallons. Its price is set by traders all over the world, around the clock.
lines.say: A barrel of oil is forty-two gallons, and its price is set by traders all over the world, around the clock.

lines.text: Think of it as one giant auction. Whoever needs a barrel most, and pays most, gets it.
lines.say: Think of it as one giant auction. Whoever needs a barrel the most, and pays the most, gets it.

lines.text: The main benchmarks are Brent, the global one, and WTI, the US one. They usually move together.
lines.say: The main price tags are called Brent, which is the global benchmark, and W T I, the American one. They usually move together.

lines.text: On September 29, 2026, Brent settled at about $103 a barrel and WTI at about $89.
lines.say: On September twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six, Brent settled at about a hundred and three dollars a barrel, and W T I at about eighty-nine.

scene.headline: Brent settles at $102.59 as Gulf exports recover

lines.text: Now meet the players. China is the biggest buyer: a record 11.55 million barrels a day of crude imports in 2025.
lines.say: Now meet the players. China is the biggest buyer on Earth, importing a record eleven point five five million barrels of crude a day in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Japan has almost no oil of its own. In 2025, 94% of its crude imports came from the Middle East.
lines.say: Japan has almost no oil of its own. In twenty twenty-five, ninety-four percent of its crude imports came from the Middle East.

lines.text: Canada is America's main supplier. It sent 63.4% of the crude the US imported in 2025.
lines.say: Canada is America's main supplier. It sent sixty-three point four percent of the crude the US imported in twenty twenty-five.

scene.caption: Top source of US crude imports

lines.text: So why import at all? Many US refineries are built for heavier crude, like Canada's, and it's often cheaper to trade than to rebuild.
lines.say: So why does a net exporter import at all? Many US refineries are built to run heavier crude, like Canada's, and trading is often cheaper than rebuilding.

lines.text: Then there's the chokepoint. In 2024, about 20 million barrels a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz.
lines.say: Then there's the chokepoint. In twenty twenty-four, about twenty million barrels a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz.

lines.text: It's a narrow strip of water between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, and tankers have few other ways out of the Gulf.
lines.say: It's a narrow strip of water between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, and tankers have very few other ways out of the Gulf.

lines.text: That's about a fifth of all the oil the world uses. And 84% of the crude going through it was headed to Asia.
lines.say: That's about a fifth of all the oil the world uses, and eighty-four percent of the crude going through it was headed to Asia.

lines.text: So you'd think a blocked strait is mostly Asia's problem. It isn't.
lines.say: So you'd think a blocked strait would mostly be Asia's problem. It isn't.

lines.text: Here's the key. If Japan loses a tanker, it bids for oil from Texas instead. Everyone is shopping in the same store.
lines.say: Here's the key. If Japan loses a tanker from the Gulf, it bids for oil from Texas instead. Everyone is shopping in the same store.

scene.label: OIL: $103
scene.caption: One store for the whole world

lines.text: So when supply gets squeezed anywhere, the price rises everywhere, even in a country that exports oil.
lines.say: So when supply gets squeezed anywhere, the price rises everywhere, even in a country that exports oil.

lines.text: Chapter two. We've been here before.
lines.say: Chapter two. We've been here before.

lines.text: In October 1973, Arab oil producers put an embargo on the United States.
lines.say: In October nineteen seventy-three, Arab oil producers put an embargo on the United States.

lines.text: Oil nearly quadrupled, from $2.90 a barrel to $11.65 by January 1974.
lines.say: Oil nearly quadrupled, from two dollars ninety a barrel to eleven sixty-five by January nineteen seventy-four.

lines.text: Americans waited in gas lines, and prices for almost everything climbed with it.
lines.say: Americans waited in long gas lines, and prices for almost everything climbed along with it.

lines.text: In July 2008, US crude hit a record $147.27 a barrel, then crashed to around $32 by December as the financial crisis hit.
lines.say: In July two thousand eight, US crude hit a record of a hundred forty-seven dollars and twenty-seven cents a barrel, then crashed to around thirty-two dollars by December as the financial crisis hit.

lines.text: That spike squeezed drivers and airlines, and the crash showed how fast demand can vanish.
lines.say: That spike squeezed drivers and airlines, and the crash that followed showed how fast demand can vanish.

lines.text: In April 2020, with the world locked down, one oil contract actually settled at minus $37.63. Sellers paid buyers to take it.
lines.say: In April twenty twenty, with the world locked down, one oil contract actually settled at minus thirty-seven dollars and sixty-three cents. Sellers paid buyers to take it.

lines.text: Storage tanks were nearly full, so holding a contract meant taking oil nobody had room for.
lines.say: Storage tanks were nearly full, so holding that contract meant taking delivery of oil nobody had room for.

lines.text: Then gas rebounded hard. Here's the US yearly average for regular gas, 2020 to 2025.
lines.say: Then gas rebounded hard. Here's the US yearly average for a gallon of regular, from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: It went from $2.17 in 2020 to $3.95 in 2022, the peak year, after Russia invaded Ukraine.
lines.say: It went from two seventeen in twenty twenty to three ninety-five in twenty twenty-two, the peak year, after Russia invaded Ukraine.

lines.text: By 2025 it had eased to $3.10. Late that year, gas even dipped under $3 for the first time since 2021.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-five it had eased to three ten, and late that year, gas even dipped under three dollars for the first time since twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: And then came 2026.
lines.say: And then came twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Chapter three. Ripple one: the pump.
lines.say: Chapter three. Ripple one, the gas pump.

lines.text: On February 27, 2026, the day before the Iran war began, Brent was around $72 a barrel.
lines.say: On February twenty-seventh, twenty twenty-six, the day before the Iran war began, Brent was around seventy-two dollars a barrel.

lines.text: By March 31, it had peaked at $118.35, as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted.
lines.say: By March thirty-first, it had peaked at a hundred eighteen dollars and thirty-five cents, as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted.

lines.text: The price of actual physical cargoes went even higher: Dated Brent hit $144.42 on April 7, a record since 1987.
lines.say: The price for actual physical cargoes went even higher. Dated Brent hit a hundred forty-four dollars and forty-two cents on April seventh, the highest since that measure began in nineteen eighty-seven.

scene.headline: Dated Brent hits $144.42, highest on record

lines.text: So what's actually inside a gallon of gas? In 2025, crude oil was 51% of the price.
lines.say: So what's actually inside the price of a gallon of gas? In twenty twenty-five, crude oil was fifty-one percent of it.

lines.text: Getting it to the station and selling it was 18%. Taxes were 17%. Refining was 14%.
lines.say: Getting it to the station and selling it was eighteen percent, taxes were seventeen, and refining was fourteen.

lines.text: Taxes are mostly a fixed amount per gallon: 18.4 cents federal, plus about 22 cents from states on average.
lines.say: Taxes are mostly a fixed amount per gallon, eighteen point four cents federal, plus about twenty-two cents from states on average.

lines.text: So when crude jumps, taxes don't, and crude's slice of the gallon gets even bigger.
lines.say: So when crude jumps, taxes don't jump with it, and crude's slice of the gallon gets even bigger.

lines.text: Crude is the biggest piece, and it's the piece that moves the most. There's a simple rule for it.
lines.say: Crude is the biggest piece, and it's also the piece that moves the most. Luckily, there's a simple rule for it.

lines.text: Every $1 rise in a barrel adds about 2.4 cents to a gallon, because one dollar spread over 42 gallons is 2.4 cents.
lines.say: Every one-dollar rise in a barrel adds about two point four cents to a gallon, because one dollar spread over forty-two gallons is two point four cents.

lines.text: Brent went from about $72 on February 27 to about $103 on September 29. Call it $30 more.
lines.say: Brent went from about seventy-two dollars on February twenty-seventh to about a hundred and three on September twenty-ninth. Call it thirty dollars more.

lines.text: Thirty times 2.4 cents is 72 cents a gallon, and that's just the crude, before refining, trucks and taxes.
lines.say: Thirty times two point four cents is seventy-two cents a gallon, and that's just the crude, before refining, trucking and taxes.

lines.text: Here's what that looked like at the pump in 2026, month by month, from January to August.
lines.say: Here's what that looked like at the pump in twenty twenty-six, month by month, from January through August.

lines.text: From $2.81 in January to $4.48 in May. That was the third-highest monthly average on record, behind only June and July 2022.
lines.say: It went from two eighty-one in January to four forty-eight in May. That was the third-highest monthly average on record, behind only June and July of twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: By September 24, AAA said the national average was the highest it has ever been for that time of year.
lines.say: By September twenty-fourth, triple A said the national average was the highest it has ever been for that time of year.

scene.headline: Gas at $4.48, highest ever for the time of year

lines.text: Now make it personal. Take a 15-gallon tank.
lines.say: Now let's make it personal. Take a fifteen-gallon tank.

lines.text: At $4.465 on September 28, 2026, that's $66.98. A year earlier, at about $3.12, it was $46.77.
lines.say: At four forty-six and a half on September twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six, that's sixty-six ninety-eight. A year earlier, at about three twelve, it was forty-six seventy-seven.

lines.text: That's $20.21 more per fill-up. Once a week for a year at that gap, it's about $1,050.
lines.say: That's twenty dollars and twenty-one cents more per fill-up. Once a week for a year at that same gap, it adds up to about one thousand fifty dollars.

scene.label: Extra per year, weekly fill-ups
scene.sub: $20.21 x 52 weeks, at the Sept 2026 gap

lines.text: And gas is the ripple you see. The ones you don't see are bigger than you'd think.
lines.say: And gas is the ripple you can see. The ones you don't see are bigger than you'd think.

lines.text: Chapter four. Ripple two: trucks and planes.
lines.say: Chapter four. Ripple two, trucks and planes.

lines.text: Almost everything you buy rode on a diesel truck at some point. And diesel hit a record.
lines.say: Almost everything you buy rode on a diesel truck at some point, and diesel just hit a record.

scene.label: diesel: $6.53
scene.caption: Everything in here came by truck

lines.text: In the week of September 21, 2026, US diesel averaged $6.529 a gallon, the highest in EIA records going back to 1994.
lines.say: In the week of September twenty-first, twenty twenty-six, US diesel averaged six dollars and fifty-three cents a gallon, the highest in E I A records going back to nineteen ninety-four.

lines.text: A week later it was $6.382, still $2.63 more than a year earlier.
lines.say: A week later it was six thirty-eight, still two dollars and sixty-three cents more than a year earlier.

lines.text: Diesel is also what turns into heating oil. The price of fuel oil in the August 2026 inflation report was up 52% in a year.
lines.say: Diesel's close cousin is heating oil, and in the August twenty twenty-six inflation report, fuel oil prices were up fifty-two percent in a year.

scene.label: Fuel oil prices, Aug 2026 vs year ago

lines.text: Trucking companies pass fuel costs along through surcharges, so a shipping bill can rise without the product changing at all.
lines.say: Trucking companies pass fuel costs along through fuel surcharges, so a shipping bill can rise without the product itself changing at all.

lines.text: That's why the price of the thing you order online can stay flat while delivery quietly costs more.
lines.say: That's why the price of the thing you order online can stay flat while the delivery quietly costs more.

lines.text: Planes are even more exposed. In 2025, fuel was about a quarter of airline operating costs.
lines.say: Planes are even more exposed. In twenty twenty-five, fuel was about a quarter of an airline's operating costs.

lines.text: So when jet fuel jumps, fares follow. In August 2026, airline fares were up 23.4% from a year earlier.
lines.say: So when jet fuel jumps, fares follow. In August twenty twenty-six, airline fares were up twenty-three point four percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Compare that with overall inflation that month: 3.4%. Energy as a whole was up 16.3%.
lines.say: Compare that with overall inflation that month, which was three point four percent. Energy as a whole was up sixteen point three.

scene.title: Prices vs a year ago, Aug 2026

lines.text: Gasoline itself was up 27.4%. So oil wasn't the whole inflation story, but it was the loudest part.
lines.say: Gasoline itself was up twenty-seven point four percent. So oil wasn't the whole inflation story, but it was the loudest part of it.

lines.text: Oil-importing countries feel it even harder, because they buy oil with dollars they have to earn first.
lines.say: Oil-importing countries feel it even harder, because they have to buy that oil in dollars they earn first.

lines.text: Chapter five. Ripple three: plastics and food.
lines.say: Chapter five. Ripple three, plastics and food.

lines.text: A barrel doesn't just become gasoline. Refineries split it into lots of products.
lines.say: A barrel doesn't just become gasoline. Refineries split it into a whole bunch of products.

lines.text: From 42 gallons of crude, US refineries made about 19.6 gallons of gasoline, 12.5 of diesel and heating oil, and 4.4 of jet fuel.
lines.say: From forty-two gallons of crude, US refineries made about nineteen point six gallons of gasoline, twelve point five of diesel and heating oil, and four point four of jet fuel.

lines.text: The rest becomes things like asphalt, lubricants, and the raw materials for plastics. That's why the total comes out to about 45 gallons.
lines.say: The rest becomes things like asphalt, lubricants, and raw materials for plastics. Processing makes it expand, so the total comes out to about forty-five gallons.

lines.text: Plastic packaging is made from oil and gas. In Europe, polyethylene prices rose an estimated 70 to 80% from February to April 2026.
lines.say: Plastic packaging is made from oil and gas. In Europe, polyethylene prices rose an estimated seventy to eighty percent between February and April twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Polyethylene is the most common plastic there is, the stuff of grocery bags, milk jugs and shrink wrap.
lines.say: Polyethylene is the most common plastic there is. It's the stuff of grocery bags, milk jugs and shrink wrap.

lines.text: That's the stuff in bottles, bags and food wrap. Packaging makers pass that cost to brands, and brands pass it to shelves.
lines.say: That's the stuff in bottles, bags and food wrap. Packaging makers pass that cost on to brands, and brands pass it on to store shelves.

lines.text: Food gets hit too, through fertilizer. Nitrogen fertilizer is made with natural gas, and much of it ships from the Gulf.
lines.say: Food gets hit too, through fertilizer. Nitrogen fertilizer is made with natural gas, and a lot of it ships out of the Gulf.

lines.text: The Middle East is nearly a quarter of world urea exports. By April 2026, urea topped $850 a ton, up 80% since February.
lines.say: The Middle East makes nearly a quarter of the world's urea exports. By April twenty twenty-six, urea topped eight hundred fifty dollars a ton, up eighty percent since February.

lines.text: That was the highest urea price since April 2022. Farmers buy it months before a harvest, so the cost shows up later.
lines.say: That was the highest urea price since April twenty twenty-two. Farmers buy it months before a harvest, so the cost shows up later.

lines.text: Add diesel for tractors and trucks, plus plastic for packaging, and food has three oil ripples stacked up.
lines.say: Add diesel for tractors and trucks, plus plastic for packaging, and food ends up with three oil ripples stacked on top of each other.

lines.text: But here's the surprise. In August 2026, grocery prices were up just 2.2% from a year earlier.
lines.say: But here's the surprise. In August twenty twenty-six, grocery prices were up just two point two percent from a year earlier.

scene.title: Price change vs year ago, Aug 2026

lines.text: Gas moves in days. Food moves slowly, because farm costs, contracts and competition all sit in between.
lines.say: Gas moves in days. Food moves slowly, because farm costs, contracts and competition all sit in between.

lines.text: That's the real shape of an oil shock: fast at the pump, then a slower wave through everything else.
lines.say: That's the real shape of an oil shock. It's fast at the pump, and then it's a slower wave through everything else.

lines.text: And nobody can reliably say where oil goes next. It swings on wars, weather, and what one tanker does in one strait.
lines.say: And nobody can reliably say where oil goes next. It swings on wars, on weather, and on what one tanker does in one narrow strait.

lines.text: What you can do is understand the chain, so the next price jump isn't a mystery.
lines.say: What you can do is understand the chain, so the next price jump isn't a mystery.

lines.text: Chapter six. The recap.
lines.say: Chapter six. Let's recap.

lines.text: Oil has one world price. Even a net exporter like the US pays it.
lines.say: Oil has one world price, and even a net exporter like the US pays it.

lines.text: Every $1 on a barrel is about 2.4 cents on a gallon. In 2026, that turned into gas above $4.
lines.say: Every dollar on a barrel is about two point four cents on a gallon, and in twenty twenty-six, that turned into gas above four dollars.

lines.text: Then it spreads: record diesel, airfares up 23.4%, and pricier plastic and fertilizer.
lines.say: Then it spreads, with record diesel, airfares up twenty-three point four percent, and pricier plastic and fertilizer.

lines.text: And food is the slowest ripple: up 2.2% in a year while gas was up 27.4%.
lines.say: And food is the slowest ripple, up two point two percent in a year while gas was up twenty-seven point four.

lines.text: So the next time a tanker makes the news, you'll know exactly how it finds its way to your receipt.
lines.say: So the next time a tanker makes the news halfway around the world, you'll know exactly how it finds its way onto your receipt.

post.title: America Sells Oil, So Why Did Gas Hit $4.47? How Oil Ripples Into Everything You Buy
post.ig: America exports more oil than it imports. Gas still hit $4.47. Here's why.
post.tiktok: The US is a net oil exporter, and gas still hit $4.47 in Sept 2026. One world price explains it.
post.yt_desc:
The US has exported more petroleum than it imports every year since 2020, yet regular gas averaged about $4.47 a gallon on September 28, 2026. This video follows one barrel of oil from the Strait of Hormuz to your receipt: why oil has one world price, the history from the 1973 embargo to 2026, the simple rule that every $1 on a barrel adds about 2.4 cents to a gallon, and how the shock spreads into record diesel, airfares up 23.4%, plastic packaging and fertilizer. With real math on a 15-gallon fill-up.
